**How to Assess Cultural Fit: A Guide for Better Hiring Decisions**


Hiring the right person is rarely just about skills. When someone joins a team and clashes with how people communicate or make decisions, the friction slows everything down. AI-powered candidate screening tools are changing how companies catch these mismatches early, helping hiring managers look beyond resumes to understand shared values and work styles before a single interview. The result is fewer costly missteps and teams that actually function well together.


Assessing cultural fit well means moving from gut instinct to grounded evidence, and that requires the right infrastructure.[Cercli's global HR system](https://www.cercli.com/) brings together data on candidate behavior, team dynamics, and organizational culture so hiring teams can make decisions based on signal, not assumption.

## Summary


- Cultural fit accounts for 89% of hiring failures, according to assesscandidates.com, yet most organizations still evaluate it through informal impressions rather than structured criteria. When cultural assessment lives in someone's gut rather than in defined, observable behaviors, the process produces inconsistent outcomes at best and costly mismatches at worst. The problem is not that organizations care too little about fit. The methods they use were never built to scale.
- Similarity bias quietly shapes hiring decisions even when interviewers believe they are being objective. A 2023 study published in the Journal of Applied Psychology found that unstructured hiring processes measurably narrow the range of candidates who advance past early screening, because interviewers default to familiarity when they lack a defined framework. Three interviewers assessing the same candidate against the same value can reach completely opposite conclusions, and neither is technically wrong. They are simply working from different mental models.
- Retention data makes the business case for cultural alignment concrete. SHRM's 2024 global workplace culture research, which surveyed nearly 20,000 workers across 19 countries, found that employees in positive cultures were almost four times more likely to stay with their employer than those in poor ones. Gallup's organizational culture indicator adds another layer, finding that employees who strongly agree they feel connected to their organization's culture are 4.3 times as likely to be engaged and 47% less likely to be actively looking for another job.
- Work samples and behavioral interviewing reduce the risk of misalignment more reliably than values-based questions alone. AIHR's cultural fit assessment research reports that 46% of new hires fail within 18 months due to cultural misalignment, and that companies with strong cultures see a 4x increase in revenue growth. Observing how candidates actually handle conflict, ambiguity, and pressure provides stronger evidence than asking them to describe their own qualities in an interview room.
- Hiring across MENA adds specific complexity that generic cultural fit frameworks are not designed to handle. Localization obligations like Emiratisation and Saudisation shape workforce planning, and organizations that conflate nationality with cultural compatibility can let evaluation standards erode. Candidates shaped by hierarchical professional environments are not automatically resistant to initiative, and structured behavioral questions cut through surface-level misreadings by focusing on what candidates have actually done rather than how comfortable they appear during an interview.
- Closing the feedback loop is where most cultural fit processes fall apart entirely. 58% of employers say assessing cultural fit is one of their biggest hiring challenges, yet very few track whether candidates selected or rejected on those grounds went on to perform or stay. Without comparing recruitment assessments against 30-, 90-, and 180-day outcomes, organizations keep making the same decisions with no evidence those decisions produce better hires.

## Why Assessing Cultural Fit Has Become More Important


**Hiring for technical skill alone** has always been a *gamble* . When teams were **smaller** and worked in the **same location** , *cultural norms* spread naturally through proximity: an organic process requiring *minimal deliberate effort* . That is **no longer** how most organizations **build their teams** .


"Hiring for technical skill alone has always been a gamble — cultural alignment is what turns individual talent into collective performance." — Hiring & Retention Insight


🎯 **Key Point:** As teams grow **more distributed and diverse** , cultural fit can no longer be absorbed passively: it must be *actively assessed* from the first interview.


⚠️ **Warning:** Organizations relying *solely* on **technical screening** risk building teams where **misalignment** , friction, and **high turnover** quietly erode performance from within.


### Why do distributed teams make cultural alignment harder to maintain?


As teams grow across cities, countries, and time zones, informal culture transmission breaks down. Unwritten rules must be clarified and reinforced through every hiring decision.[SHRM's 2024 global workplace culture research](https://www.shrm.org/executive-network/insights/shrm-report-workplace-culture-fosters-employee-retention) , surveying nearly 20,000 workers across 19 countries, found that employees in positive cultures were almost four times more likely to stay with their employer than those in poor ones. This retention signal carries direct cost implications.


### When alignment shapes performance, not just atmosphere


83% of employees who[rated their workplace culture](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9136218/) as good or excellent said they were motivated to produce high-quality work, compared with 45% of those who rated their culture poorly. Workplace culture shapes how people communicate during stress, handle disagreement, and take responsibility for mistakes. A candidate can pass every technical test yet struggle if the environment requires unfamiliar behaviors.


#### Why do informal impressions break down as hiring scales?


Most hiring teams judge culture fit through informal impressions during interviews. But as hiring grows across departments, locations, and international markets, those impressions become inconsistent. What one interviewer sees as a concern, another sees as confidence. What feels like cultural misalignment may reflect a different professional background.[Cercli's global HR system](https://www.cercli.com/) consolidates candidate information, interview feedback, and assessment results in one place, enabling hiring decisions based on shared evidence rather than scattered impressions across separate tools and inboxes.


### Why international hiring raises the stakes


The failure point is usually specificity. Organizations that[hire internationally](https://www.cercli.com/resources/applicant-tracking-system-integration) without defining which behaviors matter tend to assess cultural fit through the wrong lens, measuring similarity to existing employees rather than compatibility with the organization's genuine expectations.[Deloitte's 2024 human capital research](https://www.deloitte.com/lv/en/about/press-room/deloitte-2024-global-human-capital-trends.html) noted that hybrid and remote work have made it harder for some organizations to maintain a single, uniform culture, while 61% of surveyed US HR leaders said culture matters more in a hybrid model than in an on-site environment.


Candidates from different countries may approach hierarchy, feedback, and decision-making differently. This is not a red flag. It becomes a problem only when organizations cannot distinguish between cultural incompatibility and cultural difference.


#### What does the evidence say about cultural connection at work?


[Gallup's latest organizational culture indicator](https://www.gallup.com/471521/indicator-organizational-culture.aspx) found that employees who strongly agree they feel connected to their organization's culture are 4.3 times as likely to be engaged and 47% less likely to be actively looking for another job. When assessed well, cultural fit enables people to do their best work.


But knowing why cultural fit matters is only half the picture; the other half is where most[hiring processes](https://www.cercli.com/resources/applicant-tracking-system-functional-requirements) quietly fall apart.

## Why Traditional Approaches to Cultural Fit Can Produce Poor Hiring Decisions


**Traditional approaches** to assessing **cultural fit** fail because the *methods don't scale* . What works when a **founder personally interviews** every candidate **breaks down** as **hiring volume increases** , offices multiply, or **recruiting teams expand** .


"The informal, gut-feel methods that define culture in a startup's early days become the **single biggest source of bias** and inconsistency as organizations grow." — Hiring Research Consensus


⚠️ **Warning:** Relying on **founder-led intuition** to assess cultural fit is *not* a strategy — it's a *temporary workaround* that creates **compounding hiring errors** at scale.


**Cultural-fit assessment becomes harder to maintain as hiring volume and organizational complexity increase:**


- **Early-stage startup** → Founder personal interviews → **Not replicable at volume** .
- **Growth phase** → Expanding recruiter teams → **Inconsistent standards across interviewers** .
- **Multi-office scaling** → Distributed hiring managers → **Cultural drift between locations** .


🎯 **Key Point:** The *real* problem isn't cultural fit as a concept — it's that **traditional assessment methods** are *fundamentally unscalable* , turning what should be a **strategic advantage** into a **liability** .


### When instinct becomes the standard


The failure point is usually invisible at first. An interviewer forms a positive impression, describes the candidate as "a natural fit," and the hire moves forward. That judgment might be accurate, or it might reflect[similarity bias](https://thedecisionlab.com/reference-guide/psychology/the-similar-to-me-effect) , a shared alma mater, or simply the fact that the candidate reminded the interviewer of someone they already like. According to a 2023 study published in the Journal of Applied Psychology, similarity[bias in hiring reduces workforce diversity](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/374846837_Enhancing_diversity_and_reducing_bias_in_recruitment_through_AI_a_review_of_strategies_and_challenges) by narrowing the range of candidates who advance past early screening stages, even when interviewers believe they are being objective. The problem isn't bad intent; it's an unstructured process that lets bias operate quietly.


#### What happens when cultural fit has no shared definition?


The same issue shows up across industries and organization sizes: when "cultural fit" lives in someone's head rather than in defined, observable criteria, it becomes a moving target. One hiring manager prioritizes communication style, another weighs enthusiasm, a third reads confidence as leadership potential. Three interviewers, three different assessments, one candidate. That inconsistency produces unpredictable outcomes that damage a growing team.


#### How does an unstructured debrief process make the problem worse?


Most teams rely on post-interview conversations and informal agreement. As hiring volume increases, those conversations become harder to standardize, and whoever speaks first or most confidently can dominate.[Platforms like Cercli](https://www.cercli.com/) address this by centralizing structured evaluation criteria, interview scorecards, and candidate records, so hiring decisions rest on shared evidence rather than whoever made the strongest case in a debrief room.


### When values become decoration


Big values like "integrity" or "collaboration" are difficult to measure without first turning them into specific behaviors. A candidate who claims to value teamwork and one who fixed a failing cross-functional project to restore shared accountability both espouse the same value—only one has demonstrated it. When cultural fit interviews focus on values statements instead of behavioral evidence, organizations measure what candidates say rather than what they do. That difference matters when the role requires those values to show up under pressure, not in an interview room.


#### Why does role-specific calibration change what gets measured?


The same logic applies to role-specific fit. A senior product manager and an entry-level customer support hire may both need collaboration, but what that looks like in practice differs significantly. Using the same cultural assessment for both roles creates noise rather than consistency.[Structured behavioral questions](https://www.cercli.com/resources/automated-candidate-screening) calibrated to each role's specific demands give interviewers concrete criteria to evaluate and give candidates a fair opportunity to demonstrate actual fit rather than perform it.


That gap between performance and reality is where the most[costly hiring mistakes](https://lucasjamestalent.com/the-hidden-cost-of-bad-hiring-decisions-and-how-to-avoid-them/) hide.


## The Biggest Challenges When Assessing Cultural Fit


/ima


**Hiring mistakes** build up slowly through processes that *seem* reasonable but give[unreliable results](https://sigmundtest.com/en/ressources/blog-about-tests/sigmund/understanding-psychometric-test-reliability-and-va-06241025) . **Informal judgment** , **gut-feel assessments** , and **unstructured interviews** are *especially* prone to producing outcomes that feel confident but aren't dependable.


"Processes that seem reasonable can quietly produce **unreliable results** — and hiring teams rarely notice until the damage is done."


🎯 **Key Point:** The danger isn't a broken process; it's a *flawed* process that **looks like it's working** .


The **main problem** is *not* that organizations care too little about **cultural fit** — it's that they treat it as something that can be judged *informally* without a plan, then **trust the result anyway** .[According to assesscandidates.com](https://www.assesscandidates.com/cultural-fit-hiring/) , **cultural fit accounts for 89% of hiring failures** , making it *central* to whether a hire works. It's *not* that organizations care too little about **cultural fit** —it's that they treat it as something they can judge at all.


" **Cultural fit accounts for 89% of hiring failures** — making it the single most decisive factor in whether a hire succeeds or collapses." — assesscandidates.com


**The more structured the cultural-fit assessment, the more reliable the hiring decision and the lower the associated risk:**


- **Informal / gut-feel judgment** → **Low reliability** → **High risk** .
- **Unstructured interviews** → **Moderate reliability** → **High risk** .
- **Structured cultural-fit assessment** → **High reliability** → **Low risk** .


⚠️ **Warning:** Trusting **informal cultural fit evaluations** without a structured framework is one of the *leading* drivers of **costly hiring failures** .


🔑 **Takeaway:** When *89% of hiring failures* trace back to **cultural fit** , treating it as an afterthought isn't just careless — it's *expensive* .


### Why does informal cultural assessment keep producing bad hires?


Most organizations handle cultural assessment loosely: a hiring manager asks a few questions about working style, someone mentions the candidate seemed like a "good fit," the team agrees, and nobody documents what that means. When the hire fails six months later, there's no trail to follow. That's a process problem, not a people problem.


The failure point is usually disconnection. Cultural assessment lives separately from job requirements, interview scorecards, and hiring decisions. When those elements aren't linked, cultural evaluation becomes an opinion floating alongside the process rather than a signal informing it. Teams using a[global HR system](https://www.cercli.com/) to manage hiring workflows find that connecting structured cultural criteria directly to candidate profiles and interview stages makes evaluation more consistent, since evidence lives in the same record rather than scattered across emails and memory.


### How do you know if your cultural fit decisions are actually working?


Measuring accuracy is also a challenge.[According to assesscandidates.com](https://www.assesscandidates.com/cultural-fit-hiring/) , 58% of employers say assessing cultural fit is one of their biggest hiring challenges, yet few track what happened to candidates they selected or rejected on those grounds. Did the person hired for "strong culture fit" stay and perform well? Did the one rejected for being "a bit different" do well elsewhere? Without closing that feedback loop, organizations keep making the same decisions with no evidence they're producing good hires.


### What makes cultural fit harder to assess across different backgrounds?


Culture itself adds difficulty, particularly for teams hiring across borders. What reads as confident and direct in one environment may seem rude in another. What looks like respect may reflect a different relationship with hierarchy, not lack of initiative. Organizations building multicultural teams must distinguish between genuine misalignment with working principles and unfamiliar differences. Confusing the two doesn't protect culture—it narrows it.


The question worth sitting with is not whether your organization values cultural fit, but whether your assessment method could tell you anything useful.


## 10 Practical Ways to Assess Cultural Fit


To **assess cultural fit** , you need to **define your values in practice** , gather evidence through[multiple assessment methods](https://www.cercli.com/resources/ats-features) , and **evaluate candidates** in a *consistent* and *structured* way.


"Organizations that use **multiple assessment methods** to evaluate cultural fit make more informed hiring decisions and reduce the risk of costly mismatches." — Hiring Best Practices


**A strong cultural-fit assessment should turn abstract values into observable evidence and apply the same standards consistently across candidates:**


- **Define values in practice** → Translate culture into **observable behaviours** → Sets a **clear, measurable standard** .
- **Gather evidence** → Use multiple assessment methods across **interviews, tasks, and references** → Reduces **bias and blind spots** .
- **Evaluate consistently** → Apply the **same criteria to every candidate** → Ensures **fair, defensible hiring decisions** .


🎯 **Key Point:** **Cultural fit assessment** is *not* a gut-feeling exercise — it requires **defined values** , **structured evidence** , and **consistent evaluation** across every candidate.


💡 **Tip:** Before your next hire, document **what your values look like in action** so every interviewer is working from the *same* playbook — this is the **most critical** step most teams skip.


### 1. Define culture in observable terms first


Turn broad ideas about company culture into specific behaviors and working expectations before writing interview questions. Values like collaboration, accountability, or innovation are difficult to evaluate when everyone understands them differently. Observable behaviors give interviewers concrete criteria to evaluate, enabling consistency across a[distributed hiring team](https://www.cercli.com/resources/best-applicant-tracking-system-uk) .


Organizations often skip this step, writing job descriptions that reference "strong cultural alignment" without defining what that looks like in a Tuesday afternoon meeting or difficult client conversation. When the definition exists only in someone's head, the evaluation lives only in their gut.


### 2. Translate values into behavioral competencies


Turn organizational values into skills that candidates can demonstrate during hiring. If teamwork is a core value, explain what it means in your context: sharing information promptly, resolving disagreements without managerial involvement, and adapting your approach with different people under pressure.


This is most important for organizations with multiple people involved in hiring decisions. Without a clear plan, two interviewers assessing the same candidate on the same value may reach different conclusions, not because either is wrong, but because they're using different definitions of what that value means.


### 3. Use structured interview questions


Ask candidates the same set of questions designed around the behaviors your organization values. Structured questions enable fair comparison against consistent expectations rather than allowing each interviewer to define cultural fit individually.


Prepare behavioral and situational questions with appropriate follow-up prompts, and use interview scorecards to document evidence and assessments. Scorecards separate[evidence-based hiring decisions](https://www.academicwork.fi/en/articles/recruitment/what-is-evidence-based-recruitment) from those based on who spoke most confidently in the debrief.


### 4. Apply behavioral interviewing with discipline


Ask candidates to describe how they handled situations they actually experienced, not how they would handle them in theory. Past behavior under real conditions provides stronger evidence than self-reported qualities or theoretical answers.


Focus on situations involving conflict, feedback, failure, and ambiguity. These reveal how someone acts when uncomfortable—precisely when cultural alignment matters most. Follow up by asking what they did, why they made that decision, and what happened as a result. The "why" typically contains the most useful signal.


### 5. Add situational scenarios for roles where judgment matters


Give candidates realistic situations and ask how they would respond. This approach works particularly well for roles where communication, adaptability, or[cross-functional collaboration](https://www.simpplr.com/glossary/cross-functional-collaboration/) are central, as it surfaces how candidates approach problems before joining the organization.


Create scenarios relevant to the actual role: a disagreement with a manager, conflicting team priorities, or an ambiguous decision with no clear right answer. The goal is to understand their default reasoning process under conditions that mirror the job.


### 6. Use work samples and job simulations


Watching how people act provides better proof than asking candidates to describe their own qualities. Depending on the job, use group exercises, written communication tasks, problem-solving scenarios, or leadership simulations. Keep assessments directly related to real job requirements.


According to[AIHR's cultural fit assessment research](https://www.aihr.com/blog/cultural-fit-assessment/) , 46% of new hires fail within 18 months due to cultural misalignment. Work samples give both sides a realistic preview of how the working relationship will function.


### 7. Involve multiple interviewers and calibrate independently


Use more than one informed perspective when assessing cultural alignment. Cultural fit can collapse into one person's preferences. Multiple perspectives reduce that risk, but only when interviewers record independent assessments before discussing the candidate as a group.


The calibration step matters. When interviewers discuss a candidate before scoring, the most confident voice in the room tends to anchor everyone else's judgment. Independent scoring followed by structured comparison surfaces genuine disagreement, which gives a hiring team the most useful information.


### 8. Assess culture add, not just culture fit


Most teams assess culture by trying to match it: does this person seem like the people already here? This approach creates a slow drift toward sameness that limits the organization's ability to think differently, adapt, and grow.


Evaluate what a candidate can add to culture, not whether they fit it. Ask what perspective they bring, which experiences could strengthen the team, and whether they can work effectively within the organization's principles while adding something different. This distinction matters for growing and[multicultural organizations](https://www.hult.edu/blog/benefits-challenges-cultural-diversity-workplace/) that want shared principles without narrowing the range of thought.


### 9. Make cultural expectations transparent to candidates


Think of[cultural assessment](https://www.pmapstest.com/blog/what-is-cultural-assessment) as a two-way process. Candidates need to determine whether the organization's way of working suits them, and transparency about the company before making an offer reduces the risk of a poor fit after hiring.


#### What should organizations communicate to candidates upfront?


Explain how decisions get made, how teams communicate, what people expect regarding autonomy and flexibility, what leadership looks like, and how feedback is given and received. This matters especially when hiring internationally or remotely, where candidates cannot observe the organization firsthand before starting. Transparency about these elements mitigates risk.


#### How does centralizing recruitment workflows keep cultural criteria consistent?


Most hiring teams manage this through scattered emails, verbal conversations, and whatever the hiring manager remembers to mention. As candidate volume grows and teams become distributed, that approach quickly loses consistency.[Cercli addresses this](https://www.cercli.com/) by centralizing recruitment workflows within a[unified HR and payroll platform](https://app.cercli.com/login) , so cultural criteria, interview scorecards, and candidate communications live in one system rather than spread across disconnected tools.


### 10. Measure cultural-fit outcomes after hiring


Without measuring results, organizations cannot know whether their definition of cultural fit improves hiring decisions. Compare recruitment assessments with new-hire retention, employee engagement, early turnover, and hiring manager satisfaction at 30, 90, and 180 days.


#### What happens when cultural-fit scores don't predict retention?


If candidates with high cultural-alignment scores consistently leave within their first year, the organization should reconsider either its assessment method or its definition of cultural fit. Treat the assessment process as a hypothesis and use post-hire data to test it.[AIHR reports](https://www.aihr.com/blog/cultural-fit-assessment/) that companies with strong cultures see 4x revenue growth.


#### How do you build a cultural-fit process that holds up at scale?


The strongest cultural-fit assessment combines clear behavioral expectations, structured interviews, relevant work samples, multiple independent perspectives, and post-hire measurement that feeds back into the process. Each element checks a different failure mode, and together they create something that holds up at scale.


Complications arise when that rigorous process meets the specific[hiring realities of the MENA](https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/entities/publication/33cffd94-23d3-5dd3-93a4-10930dd2bbd2) region.


## Cultural Fit Considerations for Employers in MENA


**Hiring across MENA** is *fundamentally* different from **Western Europe** , where employment rules have become *more* similar over time. The region has its own **regulatory frameworks** , **workforce localization requirements** , and **distinct professional cultures** that employers must navigate carefully. Organizations need to separate **three things** that are *often* mixed together: **compliance obligations** , **cultural difference** , and **cultural alignment** — treating them as one is a *critical* mistake.


"The MENA region operates under its own regulatory frameworks, workforce localization mandates, and professional norms — making it *essential* for employers to distinguish between what is **legally required** , what is **culturally different** , and what represents **genuine alignment** ."


**Successful hiring across MENA requires separating legal compliance from cultural awareness and genuine values alignment:**


- **Compliance obligations** → Legal and regulatory requirements, such as **Saudization and Emiratization** → **Non-negotiable** , because failure can create legal risk.
- **Cultural differences** → Variations in communication, hierarchy, and work norms → Require **awareness, not judgment** .
- **Cultural alignment** → Shared values between employer and employee → Supports **retention and team cohesion** .


💡 **Tip:** Before assessing *cultural fit* , employers should first map out their **compliance obligations** by country — these are *non-negotiable* and must be separated from subjective cultural judgments.


⚠️ **Warning:** Conflating **cultural difference** with a lack of **cultural alignment** is one of the most *common* hiring mistakes in the MENA region — and it can lead to **biased decisions** and missed talent.


### Localization requirements belong in workforce planning, not interviews


[Emiratisation in the UAE and Saudisation](https://reaphr.com/blog/gcc-workforce-nationalisation-uae-saudi-oman-bahrain-qatar) under the Nitaqat program both shape hiring priorities. When nationality becomes a stand-in for fit, evaluation standards weaken. A structured recruitment process serves both goals: it gives organizations the visibility needed to meet localization targets while ensuring every candidate, regardless of nationality, is assessed against the same behavioral criteria. The two objectives align only when kept deliberately separate.


### Does surface-level reading explain most cultural mismatches?


A candidate who gives careful, formal answers is not necessarily less willing to work with others than someone who speaks freely. Someone shaped by a hierarchical workplace is not automatically resistant to taking initiative. Structured behavioral questions cut through this noise by focusing on what candidates have done, not how comfortable they feel in interviews. Research from the[2023 Journal of Applied Psychology](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/14413582241264619) confirms that unstructured interviews are vulnerable to surface-level misreading, with interviewers defaulting to familiarity when they lack a defined framework.


#### How do disconnected systems erode structured criteria across markets?


Most teams managing cross-border hiring across the GCC handle candidate information through spreadsheets, email threads, and disconnected systems. As headcount grows and hiring spans multiple markets, context gets lost between stages, and the structured criteria built at the start rarely survive intact through to final decision.[Platforms like Cercli](https://www.cercli.com/) bring hiring, HR, and workforce data into a single environment, keeping behavioral benchmarks visible and consistent through every stage across every market.


### What transparency does for cross-border candidates


Cross-border and remote candidates miss the informal signals that in-person candidates absorb naturally. They can't walk through the office or read the room. Employers that clearly communicate working arrangements, feedback norms, reporting structures, and management style before making an offer give candidates the information they need to make an honest choice about whether the job suits them. Transparency reduces mismatches by helping the right candidates recognize themselves in what is being described.


### Privacy is part of the candidate experience


Hiring technology now touches almost every stage of the hiring process, from screening and assessments to interview scheduling and feedback collection. Across MENA, the[UAE Personal Data Protection Law](https://u.ae/en/about-the-uae/digital-uae/data/data-protection-laws) and Saudi Arabia's Personal Data Protection Law control how candidate data is collected, processed, and retained. Organizations that treat data governance as an afterthought risk regulatory exposure and signal to candidates—particularly experienced professionals with options—that internal standards are inconsistent. Well-handled privacy practices serve as quiet employer branding.


Building teams that work well together across the GCC requires creating conditions where different people can do their best work within a shared framework. The systems required to make this real are more demanding than most organizations expect.

### What does a more connected approach to cultural fit look like?


The process begins by defining role requirements and identifying behaviors critical for success.
